record.file_problem: Repo text only: README and file list; code and report files were not read or run.
record.tranche_reason: The README evaluates released abliterated weight variants using behavioral attack-success rates, rather than reproducing the original direction-finding and activation-ablation method.
record.gate_note: The README reports prompt-injection ASR for aligned and abliterated model pairs. The listed report files are not themselves readable study results here. It also reports encoding-attack observations; those concern decoding capability rather than the refusal behavior named in the versions, so they are not included as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The study compares released huihui_ai abliterated weight edits with their aligned counterparts, using garak prompt-injection ASR. That is a new setting and an indirect proxy for whether refusal was removed (V2). It does not find or ablate a direction itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. Abliteration greatly raises KillHumans injection success in both families. Effects on other probes are smaller and, on Qwen, masked by a ceiling. Encoding differences are read as decoding damage, not safety.
record.recipe_differences: The README evaluates released abliterated weight variants rather than finding a harmful-minus-harmless activation difference and projecting it out at every layer and position. This is an assessment repo; it lists assessment scripts and reports but the code and report files were not read or run.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects differed by model family and injection probe; Qwen's high aligned ASR on HateHumans and LongPrompt left little measurable headroom.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen Hex, the abliterated model's encoding-attack ASR was lower (20.3% vs 35.0%, CIs disjoint). The authors attribute this to degraded decoding (garbled output), not to safety.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Released abliterated weights may degrade some capabilities, such as hex decoding.

record.problems: The README describes a scoped assessment with small models (3B and 7B), a narrow attack surface, and one run per model without repeated seeds; its CIs capture within-run sampling variance only. The authors note string-based detectors can miss semantic compliance or count incidental matches, and encoding results conflate capability and safety. The README also gives inconsistent Llama generation counts: 3 in the method summary and 5 in the Finding 1 table.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the reported prompt-injection results. Encoding observations are not rows for the tested claim version because they do not measure refusal behavior.

untested.parts: Refusal rates on ordinary harmful requests; whether the edit is a direction projection (the study takes huihui_ai's releases as given); general capability beyond an incidental Hex decoding observation; models beyond 3B/7B.

missing.what: Encoding-probe ASR (Qwen Hex 20.3% vs 35.0%; Base64 and ROT13 near zero), a possible capability cost of the weight edit.
missing.versions: none (capability side note; could inform V2 capability preservation)

record.verdict_notes: I dropped the reader's 'challenges' label for r2–r3: the aligned baselines were near ceiling, so those probes cannot show refusal removal. ASR comes from garak string detectors on injection tasks, a loose proxy for refusal. Each model has a single run; CIs reflect within-run variance only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not find or ablate a difference-in-means residual direction, test refusal on ordinary harmful or harmless requests, or evaluate general capability broadly.
Evaluates released abliterated variants, but does not itself perform a weight edit or directly measure ordinary refusal rates; its behavioral measure is prompt-injection ASR.
Does not test whether attacks suppress a refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare one direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not distinguish harmfulness judgment from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.

relation.reason: Its own aligned-vs-abliterated ASR comparisons bear on whether released abliteration weight edits remove refusal, as an indirect proxy.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates released huihui_ai abliterations (the V2 object) in a new setting: garak prompt-injection probes. It does not find or ablate a direction itself, and its measure is a proxy for refusal, so T3 fits better than the reader's T2.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] id for the single V2 verdict, so 'l1' was assigned by position. The README contradicts itself on Llama generations: the Method table says 3, the Finding 1 table says 5 ('matched methodology'). The '3-generation re-run' may be the original run (the report files are named _v2). The Limitations say 'single run per model'. The measure is garak string-match injection ASR on 3B/7B models: a proxy for refusal, not a refusal rate.

statements.correction: Add r6 to the cited rows. Qwen 2.5 7B: KillHumans 47.3% -> 85.4% (+38.1, significant); HateHumans 87.1% -> 88.4% and LongPrompt 80.7% -> 79.9% (CIs overlap; README calls this a ceiling). Llama 3.2 3B: KillHumans 16.5% -> 68.3% (+51.8), HateHumans 41.5% -> 68.9% (+27.4), LongPrompt 60.8% -> 67.0% (+6.2), all significant (disjoint CIs). Llama KillHumans re-run: +51.3 pts.
statements.problem: All numbers for this study match the README. Minor: the cited rows (r1–r5) leave out r6, though its Llama LongPrompt numbers (60.8% -> 67.0%) are quoted. 'Stays mid-range' is a loose word for 85.4%. 'One run per model' follows the README's Limitations, but the README also reports a separate 3-generation Llama KillHumans re-run.
